title: Teaching a Model a New Skill Without Training It
summary:
An AI agent wrote new parts into a finished language model, and its benchmark score went up.

Most ways of making a language model better start with a training run. Someone collects examples, nudges billions of numbers, and hopes the model gets better at one task without getting worse at everything else. This paper asks a stranger question: what if the model is never trained at all?

The renovation problem

Think of a language model as a finished house. You can improve one room by knocking down walls and rebuilding. That works, but every change touches the whole house. You need many examples, a lot of compute, and a careful check that the bathroom still works after you rebuild the kitchen.

Fine-tuning, the usual way to specialize a model, is this kind of renovation. It changes many weights at once, guided by labeled answers.

The aha moment

The central idea fits in one sentence: an AI agent can write new capabilities into a pretrained model by adding small parts inside its existing layers, without backpropagation and without fitting any weight to the answers of task examples.

The diagram below shows the flow. The model stays frozen. The agent adds parts. Each part is gated, so it is meant to matter mainly when its input matches the subtask it was written for.

Picture a locksmith cutting a hidden side door into a finished house. The door opens only for one key shape, and the rest of the house keeps working as before. The analogy breaks at one point: the new parts are not a separate door. They are fused into the same computation, so they run on every input.

How it works

Inside each layer of a language model are two kinds of components. Attention heads decide which earlier words matter for predicting the next word. MLP neurons transform the information after that.

The agent adds new attention heads and neurons next to the existing ones. Each new part has a gate that decides how much it adds. The gate is meant to let the part act when the input looks like the subtask it was written for, and to keep it small otherwise. The abstract does not say how the gate behaves in detail.

The agent works under a tight budget: 50 model passes. It sees no validation or test instances, so it cannot tune against the answers it will be graded on.

The agent wrote modules for six subtasks from BIG-Bench Hard, a standard reasoning benchmark, and they were composed into one model. For Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, the normalized BBH score rose from 19.95 to 41.05. For Gemma-3-1B-it, it rose from 10.25 to 32.86. The abstract also gives a figure of at most 35.01 for the larger 7B Qwen model. It does not say whether that model also received the agent's parts, so read the number as context rather than a head-to-head.

The chart below shows the gap for the two small models.

The fair worry: did anything else break?

Adding parts to a model can disturb everything else. The authors checked this directly. On 1,023,000 WikiText tokens, the composed model's next-token distribution was identical to the original's, with a KL divergence of exactly 0. The composed models gave identical answers on 15,845 items from five other tests, and identical scores on the other 18 BBH subtasks.

That is the most interesting part of the result for us. The capability was added, and the behavior that was not targeted stayed the same on the checks that were run.

Arithmetic the model never ran

The agent also wrote exact multiplication up to 20 digits. During the search, the model itself was run only on problems up to 6 digits. On the lengths it never ran, the sealed test score was 100.0% in both models. A LoRA fine-tune with the same 50-pass budget reached at most 2.1%.

The authors committed the sealed test to git before the first session, with manifests timestamped in Bitcoin. A frozen evaluator ran the sealed test once.

Why it matters

Most teams treat a model as fixed, and training as the only way to change it. This work suggests a different option for narrow skills: a targeted add-on written into the model, with a clear check that the rest of its behavior holds.

For a team that needs one reliable skill and cannot afford a training run, this is worth testing against a fine-tune on their own tasks. That is our reading, not a claim the paper makes.

Limits

Demonstrated by the authors: the BBH gains for two small models, the unchanged WikiText distribution, the unchanged scores on other tests, and the 20-digit multiplication result. These are reported in the abstract with the settings above.

Not shown or unclear:

  • The study covers two small models, plus one 7B comparison.
  • The six BBH subtasks were chosen by the authors. The abstract does not show generalization to other tasks.
  • The abstract does not say how much compute or human effort the agent search costs.
  • The LoRA baseline used the same budget. A different baseline might do better.
  • This is an arXiv preprint. We have not seen peer review.

Our inference: the unchanged WikiText result is the strongest reason to take the approach seriously. It is a check on a large sample, not a proof that nothing else changed.

This article draws on the paper's abstract. The full method and experiments were not checked in detail here.

Sources

  • "Don't Train It, Write It: An AI Agent Writes New Capabilities into Language Model Weights." Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28483

title: Vetting a UK supplier in a few lines of code
summary:
Before you raise a purchase order, onboard a supplier, or take on a new client, you usually want a few facts from the public register. Is the company still active? Are its accounts overdue? Have several directors just resigned? Are there outstanding charges?

You can pull that from official Companies House data without wiring up the Public Data API yourself. This tutorial uses the UK Company Check & Risk Score API from UK Data APIs. Search by name, then make one further call for a 0â€“100 risk score, a verdict, and plain-English reasons.

The score is a first pass for KYB and due diligence, not a credit rating and not legal advice. Officer and owner names, dates of birth (month and year only) and addresses are personal data from the public register. You must only use them for a lawful purpose under UK GDPR.

What you will build

A short script that:

  1. Searches Companies House by company name.
  2. Takes the first matching company number.
  3. Runs the one-call /check endpoint.
  4. Prints the score, verdict, reasons and a few summary figures.

A useful test number is Tesco PLC, 00445790. Company numbers are 8 characters. Prefixes such as SC, NI and OC are allowed. Shorter numeric numbers are left-padded, so 445790 becomes 00445790.

Get a RapidAPI key

  1. Open the API listing and subscribe. The BASIC plan is $0, with 100 requests included each month and then $0.008 per request, so you can try it without a monthly fee.
  2. Copy your RapidAPI key from the playground or your RapidAPI dashboard.

Every request needs two headers:

  • X-RapidAPI-Key â€” your key
  • X-RapidAPI-Host â€” uk-company-check-risk-score.p.rapidapi.com

Keep the key in an environment variable:

export RAPIDAPI_KEY="your_rapidapi_key_here"

Endpoints

All routes are GET only. The base URL is https://uk-company-check-risk-score.p.rapidapi.com.

Path What it returns
/v1/search?q= Search companies by name or number. q is required and must be at least 2 characters. Returns status, type, incorporation date and registered office
/v1/company/{number} Profile: status, type, jurisdiction, SIC codes, registered office, accounts and confirmation statement due dates with overdue flags, charges and insolvency-history flags, and previous names
/v1/company/{number}/officers Current and resigned officers (directors, secretaries and other roles)
/v1/company/{number}/owners Persons with significant control (PSCs)
/v1/company/{number}/filings Filing history (accounts, confirmation statements, officer changes and more)
/v1/company/{number}/charges Registered charges, including outstanding and satisfied
/v1/company/{number}/check One-call KYB check: 0â€“100 score, verdict and plain-English reasons. Counts as one request on your plan
/v1/officers/search?q= Search officers by name. q is required and must be at least 2 characters

Search and list endpoints accept optional paging: start_index (default 0) and items_per_page (maximum 100; default 20 on search endpoints and 35 on officers, owners, filings and charges). If a company exists but has no charges or owners, those list endpoints return an empty list rather than 404.

Search, then check, in JavaScript

This works in Node.js 18+ with the built-in fetch API.

const HOST = "uk-company-check-risk-score.p.rapidapi.com";
const headers = {
  "X-RapidAPI-Key": process.env.RAPIDAPI_KEY,
  "X-RapidAPI-Host": HOST,
};

async function get(path) {
  const res = await fetch(`https://${HOST}${path}`, { method: "GET", headers });
  const data = await res.json();
  if (!res.ok) {
    const err = data.error || {};
    throw new Error(`${res.status} ${err.code || "ERROR"}: ${err.message || res.statusText}`);
  }
  return data;
}

const search = await get(`/v1/search?q=${encodeURIComponent("TESCO PLC")}&items_per_page=5`);
const match = search.items[0];
console.log(`${match.company_name} (${match.company_number}) â€” ${match.company_status}`);

const check = await get(`/v1/company/${match.company_number}/check`);
console.log(`Score: ${check.score} (${check.verdict})`);
for (const reason of check.reasons) console.log(`- ${reason}`);
console.log(
  `Officers: ${check.summary.active_officers}, overdue accounts: ${check.summary.accounts_overdue}, outstanding charges: ${check.summary.outstanding_charges}`
);

Save it as company-check.js and run node company-check.js.

If you already have the company number, skip the search and call /v1/company/00445790/check directly.

Reading the check response

A successful check for Tesco PLC looks like this (counts and dates change as the register is updated):

{
  "company_number": "00445790",
  "company_name": "TESCO PLC",
  "company_status": "active",
  "score": 92,
  "verdict": "LOOKS_OK",
  "reasons": [
    "2 outstanding charges are registered against the company."
  ],
  "flags": [
    {
      "code": "OUTSTANDING_CHARGES",
      "severity": "info",
      "message": "2 outstanding charges are registered against the company."
    }
  ],
  "summary": {
    "company_status": "active",
    "company_status_detail": null,
    "date_of_creation": "1947-11-27",
    "age_years": 79,
    "accounts_overdue": false,
    "accounts_next_due": "2027-08-26",
    "confirmation_statement_overdue": false,
    "confirmation_statement_next_due": "2027-07-02",
    "active_officers": 12,
    "appointments_last_12_months": 1,
    "resignations_last_12_months": 1,
    "director_appointments_last_12_months": 1,
    "director_resignations_last_12_months": 1,
    "filings_count": 8373,
    "outstanding_charges": 2
  },
  "source": "Contains public sector information from Companies House licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.",
  "privacy": "Officer and owner names, dates of birth (month and year) and addresses are personal data from the public register. You must only use them for a lawful purpose under UK GDPR.",
  "generated_at": "2026-11-11T11:59:31.359Z"
}

Verdicts are LOOKS_OK (80â€“100), CHECK_CAREFULLY (55â€“79) and HIGH_RISK (below 55). The score starts at 100 and is reduced for warning signs such as:

  • dissolved, liquidation or administration status (and similar distressed states)
  • a proposal to strike off
  • insolvency history
  • overdue accounts or confirmation statement
  • a company less than 12 months old
  • high director turnover or recent resignations
  • no active officers
  • no filings
  • outstanding charges

flags give you a machine-readable code and severity (high, medium or info) as well as the message. Outstanding charges on a large, long-established company are often routine financing, which is why a couple of charges may only be an info flag and still leave a LOOKS_OK verdict. Overdue accounts or a strike-off proposal should get more attention.

A trimmed search result for q=TESCO PLC looks like this:

{
  "query": "TESCO PLC",
  "total_results": 356,
  "start_index": 0,
  "items_per_page": 3,
  "items": [
    {
      "company_number": "00445790",
      "company_name": "TESCO PLC",
      "company_status": "active",
      "company_type": "plc",
      "date_of_creation": "1947-11-27",
      "date_of_cessation": null,
      "address_snippet": "Tesco House, Shire Park, Kestrel Way, Welwyn Garden City, United Kingdom, AL7 1GA"
    }
  ]
}

Do not assume the first hit is the right legal entity. Several similarly named companies often appear. Match on name, status, type and registered office before you run the check, especially in an onboarding form.

The same flow in Python 

import os
import requests

HOST = "uk-company-check-risk-score.p.rapidapi.com"
headers = {
    "X-RapidAPI-Key": os.environ["RAPIDAPI_KEY"],
    "X-RapidAPI-Host": HOST,
}

def get(path):
    res = requests.get(f"https://{HOST}{path}", headers=headers, timeout=20)
    data = res.json()
    if not res.ok:
        err = data.get("error", {})
        raise SystemExit(f"{res.status_code} {err.get('code')}: {err.get('message')}")
    return data

search = get("/v1/search?q=TESCO%20PLC&items_per_page=5")
match = search["items"][0]
print(f"{match['company_name']} ({match['company_number']}) â€” {match['company_status']}")

check = get(f"/v1/company/{match['company_number']}/check")
print(f"Score: {check['score']} ({check['verdict']})")
for reason in check["reasons"]:
    print(f"- {reason}")

Install the one dependency with pip install requests, then run python company-check.py.

To go deeper after the score, call /v1/company/{number} for SIC codes and due dates, /officers and /owners for people, /filings for recent accounts and confirmation statements, and /charges for the charge list (status, created_on, persons_entitled). Keep the privacy notice in mind whenever you store or display those fields.

Errors and caching

Errors are returned as { "error": { "code": "...", "message": "..." } }.

HTTP Code When
400 BAD_QUERY q is missing or shorter than 2 characters on /v1/search or /v1/officers/search
400 BAD_COMPANY_NUMBER Not a valid 8-character UK number (including prefixes such as SC, NI or OC)
401 UNAUTHORISED The request did not come through RapidAPI with a valid subscription
404 COMPANY_NOT_FOUND No company exists for that number
429 RATE_LIMITED The Companies House rate limit was reached â€” retry in a few minutes
502 UPSTREAM_ERROR Companies House did not respond

Results are cached to stay within the official Companies House limit of 600 requests per 5 minutes:

  • Company profile, officers, owners and charges: 6 hours
  • Filing history: 24 hours
  • Company and officer search: 1 hour

generated_at is the time the response was built. Cached responses may include an X-Cache: HIT header.

Pricing, licence and privacy

Prices are in USD, as shown on RapidAPI. Always check the pricing tab for current limits.

Plan Price / month Requests / month
BASIC $0 100, then $0.008 per extra request
PRO $9.99 2,000
ULTRA $24.99 10,000
MEGA $79 50,000

Data comes from the Companies House Public Data API and is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0. If you display or redistribute the data, keep this attribution:

Contains public sector information from Companies House licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

Every successful response also includes a privacy notice about personal data from the register. If you display or redistribute that data, keep the notice and only use the data for a lawful purpose under UK GDPR.

Complete Node.js and Python examples, including search-then-check and error handling, are in the accompanying example repository. Subscribe on the RapidAPI listing, set RAPIDAPI_KEY, and vet a company in a couple of requests.

summary:
Buying a used car in the UK usually starts with a registration plate and a few questions. Is the MOT still valid? Has the recorded mileage ever gone down? How many tests has it failed?

You can answer those from official DVSA MOT history without building your own integration with the DVSA trade API. What you will build

title: How to Build an InSAR Error Budget That Survives Review
summary:
How to Build an InSAR Error Budget That Survives Review

Every deformation number in an InSAR report is an estimate. Reviewers increasingly refuse an estimate without an uncertainty statement attached, and the error budget is that statement made systematic: list every mechanism that corrupts the measurement, assign each a realistic one-sigma magnitude, and combine them into a single total with an explicit breakdown.

The method is short enough to state plainly. If the error sources are statistically independent, their variances add:

σ_total = √( Σ σᵢ² )

The share of each source is its variance divided by the total variance, so shares always sum to 100% and the dominant mechanism is the one whose square dominates. That last observation is the practical payoff: quadrature combination forgives moderate uncertainty in minor sources, but the largest source sets the floor. Halving a 6 mm atmospheric term buys you far more than eliminating a 1 mm orbit term entirely.

The five standard sources

A surface-deformation budget for Sentinel-1-style small-baseline processing usually starts here:

Source What drives it Typical behaviour
DEM error Residual topography phase Suppressed by short perpendicular baselines; modest with a small-baseline strategy
Orbit error Residual satellite-position uncertainty Small with precise orbit products (e.g. POEORB); shows as long-wavelength ramps
Atmospheric delay Turbulent wet delay + stratified troposphere Often the heaviest term; several mm/epoch in humid or high-relief terrain
Decorrelation noise Temporal/geometric coherence loss Depends on land cover, interval and baseline spread; shrinks as the archive grows
Incidence-angle error Projection geometry assumptions Matters when converting line-of-sight to a vertical or slope-parallel quantity

The default magnitudes you find in tools and templates are screening values, not your project's truth. Before you defend a number, edit every line to match your baseline distribution, coherence levels and correction models.

Where the budget earns its keep

In the QA section of a monitoring report. Each deformation rate should carry a stated uncertainty with a defensible breakdown, not a single hand-waved accuracy figure.

At the pre-award stage. When someone asks "how precise will InSAR be on this site?", the budget tells you which investments actually move the total: weather-model atmospheric correction (ERA5 or GACOS-class products), a better DEM, or a longer archive.

When comparing configurations. Compute the budget twice — with and without atmospheric correction, at two incidence angles — and the contribution chart quantifies the improvement instead of describing it qualitatively.

The three limits you must state

A budget is a design-stage expectation, and this is where careless reports get pulled apart.

  1. It is not evidence of achieved accuracy. A budget predicts expected error. Achieved accuracy comes from validating against real observations — for example with a GNSS cross-validation — not from the budget itself.
  2. Correlated errors do not add in quadrature. If two terms share a driver — say DEM error and incidence-angle error both stem from one bad geolocation — the RSS model underestimates the total. Merge them or widen one honestly.
  3. Velocity-calibrated defaults are wrong for single-epoch claims. Defaults that suit velocity work can misrepresent a single-epoch measurement. Re-derive each term for the quantity you are actually reporting.

A repeatable workflow

  1. Decide the quantity and unit: millimetres for a single epoch, or mm/yr for a velocity.
  2. List the sources relevant to your processing chain — the five above are a starting set, not a dogma.
  3. Assign a one-sigma magnitude to each with a justification you can cite.
  4. Combine in quadrature and compute each source's variance share.
  5. Read the share chart: spend effort where it is fat, ignore the cosmetic terms.
  6. Write the summary into the report, then validate the result against independent measurements.

A tool that performs steps 4–5 and writes the summary paragraph is available in the InSAR workbench; the time-series tool is where the deformation estimates being budgeted come from. Calculations run locally in the browser — no monitoring data leaves your machine.

FAQ

Q: What is an InSAR error budget?
A: A systematic statement of expected measurement uncertainty: list each error mechanism, assign a one-sigma magnitude, combine independent variances in quadrature, and show which sources dominate.

Q: Why do variances add instead of uncertainties?
A: For statistically independent errors, variances (squared sigmas) add. Total uncertainty is the square root of the sum of squared terms — root-sum-square, or quadrature.

Q: Does halving every error source halve the total?
A: No. The largest term sets the floor. Reducing a dominant atmospheric term matters far more than removing a minor orbit term; use the variance share to choose.

Q: Can I use the budget as my report's accuracy figure?
A: No. It is a design-stage expectation of error, not a validation result. Achieved accuracy must come from comparison with real observations such as GNSS.

Q: What if my error sources are correlated?
A: Then quadrature is invalid and will understate the total. Merge correlated terms into one or widen one honestly to cover the shared driver.

Q: Are the default magnitudes safe to use?
A: Only as screening values. They reflect typical small-baseline Sentinel-1 processing; edit each term to match your baselines, coherence and corrections.

Q: Which source usually dominates?
A: Atmospheric delay in many humid or high-relief settings, but it is site- and configuration-dependent — always read the contribution shares rather than assuming.

Q: Does the budget tool upload my data?
A: No. The calculators run locally in the browser; no deformation data is sent to a server.

title: File Permission and Ownership
summary:
Mastering File Permissions & Ownership: chmod and chown in Bash and Python
published: false
description: A practical guide to managing Linux/Unix file permissions and ownership using chmod and chown in Shell scripting (Bash) and Python.
tags: linux, bash, python, devops

Managing file permissions and ownership is a foundational skill for anyone working with Linux or Unix-like servers. Whether you are deploying a web application, securing sensitive configuration files, or automating server provisioning, chmod and chown are the two commands you will rely on most.

In this guide, we will break down how chmod and chown work, and compare how to automate them cleanly using Shell scripting (Bash) and Python.

1. The Fundamentals: chmod vs. chown

Before writing any scripts, it helps to separate what each command controls:

  • chmod (Change Mode): Defines what actions can be performed on a file or directory (Read, Write, Execute) across three permission tiers:
    • User (u): The owner of the file.
    • Group (g): Users who belong to the file's assigned group.
    • Others (o): Everyone else on the system.
  • chown (Change Owner): Defines who owns the file or directory (both the owning user and the owning group). Changing ownership generally requires root or sudo privileges.

Permission Reference Table

Permission Symbol Octal Value Effect on a File Effect on a Directory
Read r 4 View file contents List directory contents (ls)
Write w 2 Modify or delete the file Create, rename, or delete files inside
Execute x 1 Run the file as a program/script Enter the directory (cd)

Quick Octal Math: Add the values together for each tier (User, Group, Others). For example, 755 means Owner = 4+2+1 (rwx), Group = 4+0+1 (r-x), and Others = 4+0+1 (r-x).

2. Automating chmod and chown in Shell Scripting (Bash)

In Bash, chmod and chown are native utilities, making shell scripts the fastest way to apply permissions during server setup or CI/CD pipelines.

Essential One-Liners 

# Make a shell script executable
chmod +x deploy.sh

# Set read/write for owner, read-only for group and others
chmod 644 config.yaml

# Change both user and group ownership
sudo chown www-data:www-data /var/www/html/index.html

# Recursively change ownership of an entire project directory
sudo chown -R deploy:developers /opt/myapp

Complete Bash Deployment Script

When securing a web directory, you typically want directories set to 755 (so users can traverse them) and files set to 644 (so files aren't accidentally executable):

#!/bin/bash
set -e  # Exit immediately if any command fails

TARGET_DIR="/var/www/myapp"
APP_USER="www-data"
APP_GROUP="www-data"

# 1. Ensure the target directory exists
if [ ! -d "$TARGET_DIR" ]; then
    echo "Error: $TARGET_DIR not found."
    exit 1
fi

# 2. Update ownership recursively
echo "Assigning ownership to $APP_USER:$APP_GROUP..."
chown -R "$APP_USER":"$APP_GROUP" "$TARGET_DIR"

# 3. Apply separate permissions for directories and files
echo "Setting directory (755) and file (644) permissions..."
find "$TARGET_DIR" -type d -exec chmod 755 {} +
find "$TARGET_DIR" -type f -exec chmod 644 {} +

# 4. Grant execute permission specifically to the entrypoint script
chmod 750 "$TARGET_DIR/start.sh"

echo "Done! Permissions and ownership configured."

3. Automating chmod and chown in Python

When your automation grows into a larger CLI tool or cross-platform application, Python's built-in os, shutil, and stat modules provide clean, structured alternatives without spawning external shell subprocesses.

Key Python Functions

  1. os.chmod(path, mode) Updates permissions using Python's octal prefix 0o (e.g., 0o755). You can also combine flags from the stat module (like stat.S_IXUSR) to modify specific bits without overwriting existing permissions.
  2. os.chown(path, uid, gid) Low-level ownership change that requires numeric User ID (uid) and Group ID (gid) integers.
  3. shutil.chown(path, user=None, group=None) A high-level wrapper around os.chown() that accepts string usernames and group names directly, making it much easier to read and maintain.

Complete Python Deployment Script

Here is the exact same deployment workflow implemented in Python using pathlib and shutil:

import os
import shutil
import stat
from pathlib import Path

target_dir = Path("/var/www/myapp")
owner = "www-data"
group = "www-data"

if not target_dir.exists():
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"Target directory does not exist: {target_dir}")

try:
    # 1. Update root directory ownership and permissions
    shutil.chown(target_dir, user=owner, group=group)
    os.chmod(target_dir, 0o755)

    # 2. Walk through all subdirectories and files
    for root, dirs, files in os.walk(target_dir):
        for d in dirs:
            dir_path = os.path.join(root, d)
            shutil.chown(dir_path, user=owner, group=group)
            os.chmod(dir_path, 0o755)

        for f in files:
            file_path = os.path.join(root, f)
            shutil.chown(file_path, user=owner, group=group)
            os.chmod(file_path, 0o644)

    # 3. Safely add owner-execute (+x) permission to start.sh
    startup_script = target_dir / "start.sh"
    if startup_script.exists():
        current_permissions = startup_script.stat().st_mode
        startup_script.chmod(current_permissions | stat.S_IXUSR)

    print("Done! Permissions and ownership configured.")

except PermissionError:
    print("Error: Run this script with sudo/root privileges to change ownership.")
except LookupError as e:
    print(f"Error: Invalid user or group specified ({e}).")

4. Bash vs. Python: Which One Should You Choose?

Feature Shell Scripting (Bash) Python
Syntax & Brevity Very concise; native -R flag handles recursion effortlessly More verbose; requires manual traversal (os.walk)
Error Handling Basic exit codes ($? or set -e) Granular exception handling (PermissionError, LookupError)
Readability Can get cryptic with complex conditionals Clean, structured, and easy to unit test
Ideal Use Cases Dockerfiles, cron jobs, quick server provisioning Complex CLI tools, deployment orchestrators, APIs

Summary

  • Use Bash when you need fast, direct system commands in initialization scripts, Docker builds, or CI/CD runners.
  • Use Python when file permission logic is part of a larger application that benefits from structured error handling, logging, and maintainability.

title: Norway's company register API in Python: new limited companies by industry code, last 7 days, in a CSV (no API key)
summary:
Article type: How-to guide (one task: list the limited companies registered in Norway in the last 7 days, filtered by industry code, in a CSV)

Prerequisites: Python 3.9 or later with requests (pip install requests). No API key or account: the Brønnøysund Register Centre's open data API is free. An Apify account only if you use the hosted version at the end.

Tested on: 24 November 2026, against the live Enhetsregisteret API.

Norway's company register has a free JSON API with no key, and a short Python script can use it to list every limited company (aksjeselskap, AS) registered last week in the industry you care about. If you sell to new businesses, track start-ups in one sector or keep a market map up to date, that's the weekly question: which new companies registered, in my industry, and where are they? This guide answers it with the Enhetsregisteret API from the Brønnøysund Register Centre and saves the list as a CSV.

All the data in this post comes from one endpoint:

GET https://data.brreg.no/enhetsregisteret/api/enheter

with filters as query parameters, for example organisasjonsform=AS (legal form), fraRegistreringsdatoEnhetsregisteret=2026-11-16 and tilRegistreringsdatoEnhetsregisteret=2026-11-22 (registration date range). It returns a page of units under _embedded.enheter and a page object with totalElements and totalPages. No key, no login. The data is open under the Norwegian Licence for Open Government Data (NLOD 2.0).

How do I list new Norwegian companies by industry code with the Enhetsregisteret API?

Save this as norway_new_companies.py and run python norway_new_companies.py (IT programming and consultancy, codes starting 62) or pass another prefix, for example python norway_new_companies.py 41 for construction of buildings:

import csv
import sys
import time
from collections import Counter
from datetime import date, timedelta

import requests

INDUSTRY = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "62"   # SN2025 code prefix: 62 = IT programming and consultancy
DAYS = 7
API = "https://data.brreg.no/enhetsregisteret/api/enheter"
UA = "norway-new-companies-tutorial/1.0 (python-requests)"

session = requests.Session()
session.headers.update({"User-Agent": UA, "Accept": "application/json"})

# 1. robots.txt first. data.brreg.no closes the connection instead of answering, so there are no rules to read.
try:
    robots = session.get("https://data.brreg.no/robots.txt", timeout=30)
    print(f"robots.txt: HTTP {robots.status_code}")
except requests.ConnectionError:
    print("robots.txt: no answer (connection closed), so no rules to follow")

# 2. Every limited company (AS) registered in the last DAYS full days. One read; the industry filter is local.
until = date.today() - timedelta(days=1)
since = until - timedelta(days=DAYS - 1)
params = {"organisasjonsform": "AS", "fraRegistreringsdatoEnhetsregisteret": since.isoformat(),
          "tilRegistreringsdatoEnhetsregisteret": until.isoformat(), "size": 1000}
units, page = [], 0
while True:
    r = session.get(API, params={**params, "page": page}, timeout=60)
    r.raise_for_status()
    data = r.json()
    units += data.get("_embedded", {}).get("enheter", [])
    page += 1
    if page >= data["page"]["totalPages"]:
        break
    if 1000 * (page + 1) > 10_000:               # the API refuses size * (page + 1) above 10,000
        sys.exit("more than 10,000 results: use a shorter date range")
    time.sleep(1)
print(f"{len(units)} limited companies (AS) registered {since} to {until}")


def codes(u):
    """Up to three industry codes per company; '00.000' means 'not stated'."""
    return [u[k]["kode"] for k in ("naeringskode1", "naeringskode2", "naeringskode3")
            if k in u and u[k]["kode"] != "00.000"]


# 3. Keep the companies with an industry code starting INDUSTRY, newest first.
rows = []
for u in units:
    found = [c for c in codes(u) if c.startswith(INDUSTRY)]
    if not found:
        continue
    addr = u.get("forretningsadresse") or u.get("postadresse") or {}
    rows.append({
        "registered": u["registreringsdatoEnhetsregisteret"],
        "org_number": u["organisasjonsnummer"],
        "name": u["navn"],
        "industry_code": found[0],
        "industry": next(u[k]["beskrivelse"] for k in ("naeringskode1", "naeringskode2", "naeringskode3")
                         if k in u and u[k]["kode"] == found[0]),
        "municipality": addr.get("kommune", ""),
        "postcode": addr.get("postnummer", ""),
        "founded": u.get("stiftelsesdato", ""),
        "vat_registered": u["registrertIMvaregisteret"],
        "url": f"https://virksomhet.brreg.no/nb/oppslag/enheter/{u['organisasjonsnummer']}",
    })
rows.sort(key=lambda r: (r["registered"], r["org_number"]), reverse=True)
out = f"norway_new_as_{INDUSTRY}_{until}.csv"
with open(out, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=list(rows[0]))
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerows(rows)

print(f"  {sum(not codes(u) for u in units)} have no industry code yet (missing or 00.000 'not stated')")
print(f"wrote {len(rows)} with an industry code starting {INDUSTRY} to {out}")
for code, n in Counter(r["industry_code"] for r in rows).most_common():
    print(f"  {code}  {n:>4}")
print("  top municipalities:", ", ".join(f"{m} {n}" for m, n in Counter(r["municipality"] for r in rows).most_common(3)))
print(f"  registered for VAT: {sum(r['vat_registered'] for r in rows)}")

Output on 24 November 2026 (it took about 3 seconds):

robots.txt: HTTP 200
523 limited companies (AS) registered 2026-11-16 to 2026-11-22
  323 have no industry code yet (missing or 00.000 'not stated')
wrote 26 with an industry code starting 62 to norway_new_as_62_2026-11-22.csv
  62.100    20
  62.200     6
  top municipalities: OSLO 5, HARAM 1, ULLENSAKER 1
  registered for VAT: 1

Some rows from norway_new_as_62_2026-11-22.csv (names, org numbers and links left out):

registered,industry_code,municipality,postcode,founded,vat_registered
2026-11-20,62.100,HARAM,6264,2026-11-12,False
2026-11-20,62.100,OSLO,0484,2026-11-09,False
2026-11-20,62.100,ULLENSAKER,2050,2026-11-11,False
2026-11-20,62.200,VOSS,5705,2026-11-09,False

62.100 is computer programming and 62.200 is IT consultancy and running IT systems. Only 1 of the 26 was in the VAT register yet, which is normal for a company a few days old.

Why it's built this way:

  • Filter the legal form on the server, the industry on your side. organisasjonsform=AS brings the week down to one page of 523. The industry filter runs locally so the script can count the companies that have no code yet (the "no industry code yet" line), which a server-side filter would hide.
  • All three industry codes. A company can have up to three (naeringskode1 to naeringskode3). The script matches any of them, so a company whose second activity is programming is kept.
  • Full days only. The window ends yesterday, so a run on any day of the week covers seven complete days.
  • No sort parameter. See gotcha 4.

What should I check before I trust the list?

  1. A week of new units isn't a week of new companies. Without the organisasjonsform filter the same seven days returned 2,002 units: 895 sole proprietorships (ENK, a person trading in their own name), 523 limited companies, 164 "other legal persons" (ANNA), 126 associations (FLI), 103 foreign entities (UTLA, 17 with a Swedish business address), 109 bankruptcy estates (KBO, "konkursbo") and 27 condominium associations (ESEK). Filter on the legal form you mean.
  2. Many new companies have no industry code yet. 323 of the 523 limited companies had no code or the code 00.000 ("not stated"). It isn't only the newest week: of the AS companies registered 12 to 18 October, 360 of 752 (48%) still had none on 24 November, and 235 of 699 (34%) from 11 to 17 May. An industry filter will always undercount, so report the blanks next to the matches.
  3. The codes changed to SN2025. naeringskode=62.010, a code from the older SN2007 standard that you'll still see in older guides, returns 0 units, even for a week in November 2024. The same week has 24 under 62.100. The API's naeringskode filter matches by prefix, so naeringskode=62 returned 60 units of every legal form this week, the same 60 that a local prefix match finds.
  4. The Enhetsregisteret API's date sort isn't stable between pages. Many units share a registration date, and when you sort with sort=registreringsdatoEnhetsregisteret,desc the API doesn't keep the same order inside a date from one page to the next. Walking all 2,002 units of the week 100 at a time with that sort returned 315 repeats on 24 November; at 1,000 a page, 69 repeats. The default order and sort=organisasjonsnummer,asc returned 0 repeats.
  5. One query reads at most 10,000 units. page=100 with size=100 returned HTTP 400 ("size * (page+1) kan ikke overstige 10_000"). Since 1 January 2026 there are 87,049 new units in total, so split long ranges by month or legal form.
  6. Weekends are almost empty. Registrations by day were 416 on Monday 16 November, 302 on Tuesday 17 November, 396 on Wednesday 18 November, 382 on Thursday 19 November, 402 on Friday 20 November, 57 on Saturday 21 November and 47 on Sunday 22 November. Compare weeks, not days.
  7. Some units carry a phone number or email address. 171 of this week's 2,002 did. The script doesn't copy them; if you change it, remember they can belong to a person.

To change the task, pass another prefix (41 construction of buildings, 56 restaurants, bars and catering), or change organisasjonsform to ENK for sole proprietorships (people, so handle with care).

The hosted version (Disclosure: we built this)

We built an Apify Actor, European Company Registry API, that reads Norway's register and others in one schema. Its newCompanies mode lists companies registered in Norway, Finland and Ireland in the last N days (registeredWithinDays, up to 366) or between two dates (registeredSince and registeredUntil). Two optional filters do this post's job: legalFormCodes keeps only the legal forms you list, and activityCodePrefixes keeps a company if any of its industry codes starts with a prefix you give. Norwegian rows list every industry code the register gives the company (activityCodes, current SN2025 codes) as well as the first one, the legal form code, the VAT ID when the company is in the VAT register, and a link to the official record.

For Norway it leaves some units out by default, and doesn't charge for them. Sole traders and natural persons are always skipped. Bankruptcy estates (KBO), associations (FLI) and foreign entities (NUF and UTLA) are left out too unless you set includeOtherNorwegianEntities. Other forms, such as ANNA and ESEK, still come back unless you set legalFormCodes. Each run's SUMMARY record checks that rows returned plus rows skipped equals records read. Phone numbers and email addresses are never put in rows, and monitor mode returns only companies it hasn't returned before.

In a free local run of this input on 24 November 2026 (not on the Apify platform), it read the same 523 limited companies and returned the same 26 as the script, 20 under 62.100 and 6 under 62.200. It left out 497 with no matching code, free of charge:

{
  "mode": "newCompanies",
  "countries": ["NO"],
  "registeredSince": "2026-11-16",
  "registeredUntil": "2026-11-22",
  "legalFormCodes": ["AS"],
  "activityCodePrefixes": ["62"],
  "maxResults": 0,
  "maxResultsPerCountry": 0
}

Without the two filters, the same week returned 731 rows out of 2,002 units read. It left out 1,271: 895 sole proprietorships, 141 foreign entities, 126 associations and 109 bankruptcy estates.

What it doesn't do: the industry filter can't find companies that have no code yet (323 of the 523 this week). registeredWithinDays counts back from the time of the run, so on 15 November a value of 7 covered 8 to 15 November; give two dates for whole weeks. In monitor mode it reads at most 5,000 records per country per run. It's pay per event; prices on the Actor's Pricing tab.

European Company Registry API on Apify

Data: Enhetsregisteret, Brønnøysund Register Centre, read 24 November 2026, under the Norwegian Licence for Open Government Data (NLOD 2.0). This post and the Actor are not affiliated with or endorsed by the Brønnøysund Register Centre.

title: Resilience Patterns for LLMs: Retries, Fallbacks, and Circuit Breakers
summary:
When an LLM provider experiences an outage, rate limit spike, or degraded performance, most backend developers default to a simple solution: wrap the API call in a retry loop.

Relying solely on retries often makes outages worse. If an API returns a 429 Too Many Requests or a prolonged 500 Internal Server Error, hitting the endpoint repeatedly burns your execution quota, inflates user latency, and contributes to the "thundering herd" problem when the upstream service attempts to recover.

To build production-grade AI applications, you must separate retries from fallbacks and protect your system architecture accordingly.

Understanding Retry vs. Fallback

A retry means attempting the exact same request against the same provider. This is designed for transient failures: a dropped TCP connection, a temporary network hiccup, or a sporadic 503 error.

A fallback means routing the request to a completely different provider or a secondary model family. Fallbacks are required when the primary provider is facing a hard outage, severe throttling, or persistent API degradation.

Mixing these two concepts leads to fragile systems. Retrying a 429 status code, for instance, ignores the provider's explicit request to pause traffic.

1. Smart Retries with Exponential Backoff and Jitter

If you encounter a transient error (like a 502 or 503), do not retry immediately in a tight loop. Instead, use exponential backoff combined with jitter.

Exponential backoff increases the delay between each attempt exponentially (e.g., 1s, 2s, 4s). Jitter adds a randomized offset to prevent thousands of concurrent clients from hitting the recovering server at the exact same millisecond.

Here is a practical Python implementation using explicit backoff and error handling:

import random
import time
import openai

def call_llm_with_retry(prompt: str, max_retries: int = 3) -> str:
    base_delay = 1.0
    for attempt in range(max_retries):
        try:
            response = openai.chat.completions.create(
                model="gpt-4o",
                messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
            )
            return response.choices[0].message.content
        except (openai.APIConnectionError, openai.InternalServerError) as e:
            if attempt == max_retries - 1:
                raise e
            # Calculate exponential backoff + jitter
            sleep_time = (base_delay * (2 ** attempt)) + random.uniform(0, 0.5)
            time.sleep(sleep_time)
        except openai.RateLimitError:
            # Pass rate limit errors immediately to trigger the fallback layer
            raise

2. Multi-Provider Fallback Chains

When retries are exhausted—or when a rate limit error occurs—your execution path should immediately switch to a backup provider. For example, if your primary model is OpenAI's gpt-4o, your secondary fallback could be Anthropic's claude-3-5-sonnet.

Here is how to structure a fallback chain across different SDKs:

import os
from anthropic import Anthropic
import openai

anthropic_client = Anthropic(api_key=os.environ.get("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"))

def generate_completion(prompt: str) -> str:
    # Step 1: Try Primary Provider (OpenAI) with retries
    try:
        return call_llm_with_retry(prompt, max_retries=2)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Primary provider failed or rate limited: {e}. Executing fallback...")

    # Step 2: Fallback to Secondary Provider (Anthropic)
    try:
        response = anthropic_client.messages.create(
            model="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022",
            max_tokens=1000,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
        )
        return response.content[0].text
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Fallback provider failed: {e}")
        raise RuntimeError("All configured LLM providers are unavailable.")

3. Protecting Infrastructure with Circuit Breakers

If an LLM provider goes down completely, executing two retries and a fallback for every single incoming request adds seconds of latency to your application.

A circuit breaker tracks the failure rate of a provider over a rolling window. If the failure rate exceeds a specified threshold (e.g., 50% failures over 10 requests), the circuit "opens."

When open, the system bypasses the primary provider entirely and routes requests straight to the fallback provider. After a set cooldown period, the circuit enters a "half-open" state, sending a test request to verify if the primary provider has recovered.

Key Takeaways

  1. Never retry 429s blindly: Treat rate limits as a trigger to back off or immediately execute a provider fallback.
  2. Limit retries: Two to three attempts with jittered backoff are enough for network blips.
  3. Decouple business logic: Normalize prompts and responses so switching between OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google Gemini requires zero changes in upstream code.

title: Making an LLM do math right: tool calls plus a number auditor
summary:
Language models don't calculate, they autocomplete. Ask one for a tax amount and you get something that looks right — plausible magnitude, believable decimals — but nothing guarantees it. The fix isn't a bigger model. It's routing every figure through a real program, then checking the result with a script.

Here's the setup I use: a JSON tool definition, a sandboxed evaluator built on Decimal, a system prompt that forbids mental arithmetic, and a verifier that fails the build when one number is off. Roughly 30 minutes, intermediate level.

What you need before you start

  • Python 3.10 or newer (python3 --version) on Linux, macOS or Windows.
  • An LLM endpoint that supports tool calling (function calling) and accepts a JSON Schema tool definition. Wrapper field names differ between providers — tools, functions, tool_choice — so check the docs for yours.
  • The API key in an environment variable, e.g. export PROVIDER_API_KEY="..." (the name is provider-specific).
  • A text editor and around 50 MB of free disk for the virtual environment.
  • No GPU, no database, and no network access for the calculator itself: it runs in-process.

Quick start once everything is in place:

python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
python3 calc_tool.py "1250*0.07"
python3 verify_numbers.py answer.md

Why the model invents numbers

A model predicts the next token. There is no scratchpad where 1250 * 0.07 gets multiplied, so two things go wrong: the value drifts, and the formatting drifts (87.50000000000001 instead of 87.50). The remedy is to convert "produce a number" into "ask a program for a number", with a narrow input field so the request stays machine-checkable.

One expression per call is the design choice that pays off later: one call, one claim, one line to audit.

Step 1: describe the calculator in JSON

Create tools.json in the project root with a single tool named calculate. The description is not documentation — the model reads it to decide when and how to call the tool, so write it as instructions.

{
  "type": "function",
  "function": {
    "name": "calculate",
    "description": "Evaluate exactly one arithmetic expression and return the exact decimal result. Call this for every number that appears in the answer. Do not pass function names, percent signs or units.",
    "parameters": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "expression": {
          "type": "string",
          "description": "Arithmetic expression using digits, + - * / ** ( ) and '.', for example (1250*0.07)+80"
        }
      },
      "required": ["expression"]
    }
  }
}

Sanity check that the file parses:

python3 -c "import json;print(json.load(open('tools.json'))['function']['name'])"

Expected output: calculate.

Step 2: a safe evaluator built on Decimal

calc_tool.py parses the expression into an abstract syntax tree, walks it, and allows only five operators. Nothing reaches eval(), so a confused or malicious string can't execute anything. A character whitelist rejects non-arithmetic input before parsing even starts.

import ast, operator, re, sys
from decimal import Decimal, getcontext

getcontext().prec = 28
OPS = {ast.Add: operator.add, ast.Sub: operator.sub, ast.Mult: operator.mul,
       ast.Div: operator.truediv, ast.Pow: operator.pow, ast.USub: operator.neg}
ALLOWED = re.compile(r"^[0-9eE+\-*/(). ]+$")

def _eval(node):
    if isinstance(node, ast.Expression):
        return _eval(node.body)
    if isinstance(node, ast.Constant) and isinstance(node.value, (int, float)):
        return Decimal(str(node.value))
    if isinstance(node, ast.BinOp) and type(node.op) in OPS:
        return OPS[type(node.op)](_eval(node.left), _eval(node.right))
    if isinstance(node, ast.UnaryOp) and type(node.op) in OPS:
        return OPS[type(node.op)](_eval(node.operand))
    raise ValueError(f"unsupported node: {type(node).__name__}")

def calculate(expression: str) -> str:
    if not ALLOWED.match(expression):
        raise ValueError("expression contains characters outside 0-9 + - * / ( ) . e E")
    return str(_eval(ast.parse(expression, mode="eval")))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(calculate(sys.argv[1]))

Decimal with precision 28 is the reason 1250*0.07 comes back as 87.50 and not with a binary-float tail. Two commands tell you whether the guard works:

python3 calc_tool.py "1250*0.07"
python3 calc_tool.py "round(1250*0.07)"

The first prints 87.50. The second fails with ValueError: expression contains characters outside 0-9 + - * / ( ) . e E — that failure is the point. In the loop below the error text is handed back to the model as the tool result, so it can read the message and retry with a bare expression.

Step 3: the tool loop and a turn cap

Wiring differs per provider; the loop shape doesn't. Send the question, receive a tool call, execute it, send the result back, repeat until the model stops asking.

import json
from calc_tool import calculate

TOOLS = json.load(open("tools.json"))

def run_tool(name, args):
    try:
        return calculate(args["expression"])
    except Exception as e:
        return f"ERROR: {type(e).__name__}: {e}"

def answer(question, call_model):
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": open("system.prompt").read()},
                {"role": "user", "content": question}]
    for _ in range(6):
        resp = call_model(messages, TOOLS)   # provider SDK call goes here
        messages.append(resp.message)
        calls = resp.message.get("tool_calls", [])
        if not calls:
            return resp.message["content"]
        for c in calls:
            result = run_tool(c["name"], json.loads(c["arguments"]))
            messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": c["id"], "content": result})
    raise RuntimeError("tool loop did not converge after 6 turns")

Two details matter. run_tool returns errors as strings instead of raising, so a bad call becomes a message the model can repair rather than a crashed run. And the six-turn cap stops a model that keeps retrying the same broken expression from spinning forever.

Step 4: a system prompt that works as a contract

Save this as system.prompt and pass it as the system message.

You are a calculation assistant. Every number in your final answer must come from the calculate tool.

Rules:
1. Never do arithmetic yourself, not even for "obvious" cases like 2+2. If a number appears in your answer, it must be produced by a tool call.
2. Pass one arithmetic expression per call. Use digits, + - * / ** ( ) and decimal points only. Do not pass function names such as round(), do not pass percent signs, currency symbols or thousands separators.
3. Copy the string the tool returns into your answer exactly as returned. Do not re-round it, do not reformat it.
4. End every answer with a fenced code block tagged json, containing exactly this shape:
{"claims": [{"expression": "", "value": ""}]}
Include one entry per tool call that contributed a number to the answer.
5. If an input needed for the calculation is missing, ask for it. Never substitute 0 or 1.
6. If the tool returns an error, read the error text, fix the expression once and retry. If it fails a second time, stop and report the error text verbatim.

In short: no mental arithmetic, one expression per call, digits and operators only, copy the returned string verbatim, close with a machine-checkable claims block, ask for missing inputs instead of defaulting to 0 or 1, and repair an error once before reporting it. Two edits before use: the tool name must match the name field in tools.json, and if your product needs fixed decimal places, state the number of places in rule 3.

Step 5: audit the answer before anyone reads it

verify_numbers.py takes the answer file, pulls out the claims block, recomputes each expression with the same evaluator, and compares the result against what the model said the tool returned. On any mismatch it exits with code 1.

python3 verify_numbers.py answer.md && echo "numbers OK"

That exit code is the useful part. It drops straight into CI or a pre-publish hook, so a fabricated figure can't reach a reader silently. Because every tool call produces exactly one claim, the diff between what was computed and what was written is always one line.

Takeaway

Three small pieces — a JSON tool definition, an AST-based evaluator with Decimal, and a verifier wired to an exit code — move math from "trust the text" to "check the value". The prompt carries as much weight as the code, because the model has to agree to route every number through the tool and to emit claims that can be recomputed. One caveat: if you later serve the tool over a remote MCP server instead of importing it in-process, the trust boundary moves and the server's permissions need an audit of their own.

This article was originally published on AI Release — https://ai-release.org. If you want more hands-on write-ups like this one, they also go out on the channel: https://t.me/ai_release1.

The first prints 87.50. The second fails with ValueError: expression contains characters outside 0-9 + - * / ( ) . e E — that failure is the point. In the loop below the error text is handed back to the model as the tool result, so it can read the message and retry with a bare expression.

Step 3: the tool loop and a turn cap

Wiring differs per provider; the loop shape doesn't. Send the question, receive a tool call, execute it, send the result back, repeat until the model stops asking.

import json
from calc_tool import calculate

TOOLS = json.load(open("tools.json"))

def run_tool(name, args):
    try:
        return calculate(args["expression"])
    except Exception as e:
        return f"ERROR: {type(e).__name__}: {e}"

def answer(question, call_model):
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": open("system.prompt").read()},
                {"role": "user", "content": question}]
    for _ in range(6):
        resp = call_model(messages, TOOLS)   # provider SDK call goes here
        messages.append(resp.message)
        calls = resp.message.get("tool_calls", [])
        if not calls:
            return resp.message["content"]
        for c in calls:
            result = run_tool(c["name"], json.loads(c["arguments"]))
            messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": c["id"], "content": result})
    raise RuntimeError("tool loop did not converge after 6 turns")

Two details matter. run_tool returns errors as strings instead of raising, so a bad call becomes a message the model can repair rather than a crashed run. And the six-turn cap stops a model that keeps retrying the same broken expression from spinning forever.

Step 4: a system prompt that works as a contract

Save this as system.prompt and pass it as the system message.

You are a calculation assistant. Every number in your final answer must come from the calculate tool.

Rules:
1. Never do arithmetic yourself, not even for "obvious" cases like 2+2. If a number appears in your answer, it must be produced by a tool call.
2. Pass one arithmetic expression per call. Use digits, + - * / ** ( ) and decimal points only. Do not pass function names such as round(), do not pass percent signs, currency symbols or thousands separators.
3. Copy the string the tool returns into your answer exactly as returned. Do not re-round it, do not reformat it.
4. End every answer with a fenced code block tagged json, containing exactly this shape:
{"claims": [{"expression": "", "value": ""}]}
Include one entry per tool call that contributed a number to the answer.
5. If an input needed for the calculation is missing, ask for it. Never substitute 0 or 1.
6. If the tool returns an error, read the error text, fix the expression once and retry. If it fails a second time, stop and report the error text verbatim.

In short: no mental arithmetic, one expression per call, digits and operators only, copy the returned string verbatim, close with a machine-checkable claims block, ask for missing inputs instead of defaulting to 0 or 1, and repair an error once before reporting it. Two edits before use: the tool name must match the name field in tools.json, and if your product needs fixed decimal places, state the number of places in rule 3.

Step 5: audit the answer before anyone reads it

verify_numbers.py takes the answer file, pulls out the claims block, recomputes each expression with the same evaluator, and compares the result against what the model said the tool returned. On any mismatch it exits with code 1.

python3 verify_numbers.py answer.md && echo "numbers OK"

That exit code is the useful part. It drops straight into CI or a pre-publish hook, so a fabricated figure can't reach a reader silently. Because every tool call produces exactly one claim, the diff between what was computed and what was written is always one line.

Takeaway

Three small pieces — a JSON tool definition, an AST-based evaluator with Decimal, and a verifier wired to an exit code — move math from "trust the text" to "check the value". The prompt carries as much weight as the code, because the model has to agree to route every number through the tool and to emit claims that can be recomputed. One caveat: if you later serve the tool over a remote MCP server instead of importing it in-process, the trust boundary moves and the server's permissions need an audit of their own.

title: 7 Simple Habits to Extend Your Laptop’s Lifespan and Prevent Sudden Hardware Failure
summary:
Most laptop breakdowns do not happen overnight—they build up slowly through heat, dust, and daily charging habits. Whether you use your laptop for office work, coding, design, or studies, a few practical maintenance habits can keep your system running fast and save you from expensive motherboard or battery repairs later.

  1. Avoid Using Your Laptop Directly on Beds or Pillows
    Soft surfaces like mattresses, blankets, and cushions block the air intake vents underneath your laptop. When airflow is restricted, internal temperatures rise rapidly, drying out the thermal paste and putting extra stress on the processor and GPU. Always use your laptop on a hard, flat desk or a ventilated cooling stand.

  2. Clean Dust From Cooling Vents Every Few Months
    In dusty urban environments, lint and fine dust collect inside cooling fans and heatsinks within 6 to 8 months. If you notice your fan spinning loudly even while browsing, or the keyboard area feels unusually hot, internal dust buildup is likely blocking heat dissipation. Periodic internal cleaning prevents sudden thermal shutdowns.

  3. Follow Healthy Charging Habits for Your Battery
    Keeping a laptop plugged in at 100% constantly—or letting it drain completely to 0% every day—accelerates lithium-ion battery wear.

If your laptop brand offers a Battery Health / Conservation Mode (like Lenovo Vantage, Dell Power Manager, or MyASUS), cap charging at 80% when working mostly on AC power.

Always use a genuine, voltage-matched adapter; cheap third-party chargers can damage the charging IC on the motherboard.

  1. Open and Close the Lid From the Center
    Lifting the laptop screen from one corner puts uneven pressure on a single hinge. Over time, this cracks the plastic bezel or snaps the metal hinge mounts—one of the most common physical repairs laptops require. Always hold the top center of the lid when opening or closing it.

  2. Keep Liquids Away and Never Ignore Minor Spills
    Even a few drops of water or coffee seeping under the keyboard can corrode copper traces on the motherboard days later. If a spill happens, shut down the laptop immediately, unplug the charger, and have the board inspected before turning it back on.

  3. Upgrade RAM or SSD Before Replacing an Old Laptop
    If your 3- or 4-year-old laptop feels sluggish, you rarely need to buy a brand-new machine. Upgrading from an older hard drive to an NVMe or SATA SSD and adding extra RAM can make an older system boot in seconds and handle multitasking smoothly at a fraction of the cost of a new laptop.

  4. Get Professional Chip-Level Diagnosis When Hardware Issues Arise
